english.heading: Food Forest Design
body: Build a living food system in layers.
Grow food from tall canopy down to root crops.
Use vertical space, soil life, shade, and moisture together.
Learn how to design and establish a food forest for your farm.

heading.text: Moralo wa Food Forest

body.text: Haha tsamaiso ya dijo e phelang ka mekgahlelo.
body.backTranslation: Build a food system that lives in stages.

body.text: Lema dijo ho tloha ho canopy e telele ho isa ho dijalo tsa metso.
body.backTranslation: Plant food from the tall canopy down to the root crops.

body.text: Sebedisa sebaka sa bophahamo, bophelo ba mobu, moriti le mongobo hammoho.
body.backTranslation: Use the space of height, the life of the soil, shade and moisture together.

body.text: Ithute ho rala le ho qala food forest polasing ya hao.
body.backTranslation: Learn to design and to start a food forest on your farm.

english.heading: Why This Matters
body: A food forest grows useful plants at different heights.
Good design can combine harvests, shade and soil cover. Plants still compete for light, water and nutrients.
Plan the care you can provide and watch how the planting changes.

heading.text: Hobaneng Sena se le Bohlokwa

body.text: Food forest e hodisa dimela tse molemo bophahamong bo fapaneng.
body.backTranslation: A food forest grows good plants at different heights.

body.text: Moralo o motle o ka kopanya dikotulo, moriti le sekwahelo sa mobu. Dimela di ntse di phehisana ka kganya, metsi le nutrients.
body.backTranslation: A good design can combine harvests, shade and soil cover. Plants keep competing for light, water and nutrients.

body.text: Rala tlhokomelo eo o ka e fanang mme o shebe hore dimela di fetoha jwang.
body.backTranslation: Design the care that you can give, and watch how the plants change.

english.heading: Learning Outcomes
body: Name the seven commonly described food-forest layers.
Check plants against your site, local ecology and the approved project list.
Plan establishment and ongoing care without assuming a fixed date for harvest or canopy closure.

heading.text: Seo O Tla Ithutang Sona

body.text: Reha mekgahlelo e 7 ya food forest e hlalosoang hangata.
body.backTranslation: Name the 7 layers of a food forest that are commonly described.

body.text: Hlahloba dimela ho ya ka sebaka sa hao, tlhaho ya sebaka le lenane le amohetsweng la projeke.
body.backTranslation: Check plants according to your place, the nature of the place, and the approved list of the project.

body.text: Rala nako ya pele kamora ho jala (establishment) le tlhokomelo e tswelang pele, ntle le ho nka hore ho na le letsatsi le tsitsitseng la kotulo kapa la ho kwalana ha canopy.
body.backTranslation: Plan the early period after planting and the ongoing care, without assuming that there is a fixed day of harvest or of the canopy closing.

english.heading: The Forest Uses Every Layer
body: An indigenous forest fills the space from the highest branches to the roots.
Different plants use the light and moisture available at their level.
A food forest copies this pattern with productive species.
The result is not one crop in one row, but many useful layers growing together.

heading.text: Moru o Sebedisa Mokgahlelo o Mong le o Mong

body.text: Moru wa indigenous o tlatsa sebaka ho tloha makaleng a hodimo ho isa metsong.
body.backTranslation: An indigenous forest fills the space from the upper branches down to the roots.

body.text: Dimela tse fapaneng di sebedisa kganya le mongobo tse fumanehang boemong ba tsona.
body.backTranslation: Different plants use the light and moisture that are found at their position.

body.text: Food forest e etsisa mokgwa ona ka mefuta e hlahisang.
body.backTranslation: A food forest imitates this way with producing species.

body.text: Phello ha se sejalo se le seng moleng o le mong, empa ke mekgahlelo (layers) e mengata e molemo e melang hammoho.
body.backTranslation: The result is not one crop in one row, but many good layers (layers) growing together.

english.heading: Watch: Read the Seven Planting Layers
body: Find seven planting layers.
Tall trees form the canopy.
Smaller trees grow below it.
Then look for woody shrubs.
Herbaceous plants have soft stems.
Ground cover spreads across the surface.
Root crops grow below the surface.
Climbers use suitable supports.
These are planning layers, not fixed height bands. Choose plants and spacing for your site.

heading.text: Sheba: Bala Mekgahlelo e 7 ya ho Jala
heading.backTranslation: Look: Count the 7 Layers of Planting

body.text: Fumana mekgahlelo e 7 ya ho jala.
body.backTranslation: Find the 7 layers of planting.

body.text: Difate tse telele di etsa canopy.
body.backTranslation: Tall trees make the canopy.

body.text: Difate tse nyane di mela ka tlasa canopy.
body.backTranslation: Small trees grow below the canopy.

body.text: Ebe o batla dihlahla tse nang le lehong.
body.backTranslation: Then look for shrubs that have wood.

body.text: Dimela tsa herbaceous di na le dikutu tse bonolo.
body.backTranslation: Herbaceous plants have soft stems.

body.text: Dimela tse kwahelang mobu (ground cover) di hasana hodima mobu.
body.backTranslation: Plants that cover the soil (ground cover) spread over the soil.

body.text: Dijalo tsa metso (root crops) di mela ka tlasa bokahodimo ba mobu.
body.backTranslation: Crops of roots (root crops) grow below the surface of the soil.

body.text: Dimela tse hloang di sebedisa dintho tse loketseng tse di tshehetsang.
body.backTranslation: Plants that grow [?: climbing/that sprout] use suitable things [?dintho: things/materials] that support them.

body.text: Tsena ke mekgahlelo ya moralo, e seng dibande tse tsitsitseng tsa bophahamo. Kgetha dimela le sebaka pakeng tsa tsona bakeng sa sebaka sa hao.
body.backTranslation: These are layers of the design, not fixed bands of height. Choose plants and the space between them for your place.

english.heading: The Seven Layers
body: Think of tall canopy, smaller trees, shrubs and herbaceous plants.
Ground cover protects the surface, root crops grow below it, and climbers use suitable supports.
The heights and spacing depend on the plants and site. These are planning layers, not fixed height bands.

heading.text: Mekgahlelo e 7

body.text: Nahana ka canopy e telele, difate tse nyane, dihlahla le dimela tsa herbaceous.
body.backTranslation: Think of a tall canopy, small trees, shrubs and herbaceous plants.

body.text: Dimela tse kwahelang mobu di sireletsa bokahodimo ba mobu, dijalo tsa metso di mela ka tlasa bokahodimo boo, mme dimela tse hloang di sebedisa ditshehetso tse loketseng.
body.backTranslation: Plants that cover the soil protect the surface of the soil, crops of roots grow below that surface, and plants that climb use suitable supports.

body.text: Bophahamo le sebaka pakeng tsa dimela di ipapisitse le dimela le sebaka. Tsena ke mekgahlelo ya moralo, e seng dibande tse tsitsitseng tsa bophahamo.
body.backTranslation: The height and the space between plants depend on the plants and the place. These are layers of the design, not fixed bands of height.

english.heading: Read a Layered Planting Example
body: The original Highveld example includes Wild Fig or pecan above lemon, naartjie and black mulberry.
It places Cape gooseberry and Wild Medlar with vegetables, wild garlic, sweet potato and granadilla.
Treat this as a layout example, not permission to plant every species. Check identity, frost tolerance, mature size and local restrictions first.

heading.text: Bala Mohlala wa ho Jala ka Mekgahlelo
heading.backTranslation: Read an Example of Planting in Layers

body.text: Mohlala wa pele wa Highveld o kenyeletsa Wild Fig kapa pecan hodima lemon, naartjie le black mulberry.
body.backTranslation: A first example of the Highveld includes Wild Fig or pecan above lemon, naartjie and black mulberry.

body.text: O beha Cape gooseberry le Wild Medlar hammoho le merogo, wild garlic, sweet potato le granadilla.
body.backTranslation: It puts Cape gooseberry and Wild Medlar together with vegetables, wild garlic, sweet potato and granadilla.

body.text: Nka sena e le mohlala wa moralo, e seng tumello ya ho jala mofuta o mong le o mong. Pele, hlahloba hore semela ke sefe, frost tolerance, boholo ba ho hola ka botlalo le dithibelo tsa sebaka.
body.backTranslation: Take this as an example of a design, not a permission to plant every species. First, check which plant it is, frost tolerance, size of full growth and the restrictions of the place.

english.heading: Care Changes as Plants Grow
body: Young plants need establishment care: moisture checks, weed control and protection from damage.
As plants grow, shade and leaf litter change conditions below them.
Check competition and access. Prune, thin or adjust lower planting when observations call for it; the system does not become care-free on a fixed birthday.

heading.text: Tlhokomelo e a fetoha ha dimela di ntse di hola.

body.text: Dimela tse nyane di hloka tlhokomelo ya nako ya pele kamora ho jala (establishment care): ho hlahloba mongobo, ho laola dimela tse sa batleheng le ho di sireletsa tshenyong.
body.backTranslation: Small plants need care in the early period after planting (establishment care): checking moisture, controlling unwanted plants and protecting them from damage.

body.text: Ha dimela di ntse di hola, moriti le leaf litter di fetola maemo a ka tlase ho tsona.
body.backTranslation: As plants grow, shade and leaf litter change the conditions beneath them.

body.text: Hlahloba ho phehisana le phihlello. Seha makala, kapa etsa thinning, kapa lokisa dimela tsa ka tlase, ha seo o se bonang se hloka jwalo; tsamaiso ha e fetohe e se hloke tlhokomelo ka letsatsi le tsitsitseng la tswalo.
body.backTranslation: Check competition and access [?phihlello: access/reach/light]. Prune branches [Seha makala: cut branches], or do thinning, or tidy the understory plants [dimela tsa ka tlase: plants below/under], when what you see needs it; the system does not become one that needs no care on a fixed day of birth [?letsatsi le tsitsitseng la tswalo: fixed/steady day of birth].

english.heading: Choose for Your Site
body: Check local rainfall, frost, heat, soil and water availability before choosing plants.
Mango can suffer frost damage. Quince needs suitable winter chilling for reliable cropping.
A regional label or a sheltered corner is not enough. Confirm each plant and variety with reliable local guidance.

heading.text: Kgetha ho ya ka Sebaka sa Hao

body.text: Hlahloba pula ya sebaka, serame, mocheso, mobu le ho fumaneha ha metsi pele o kgetha dimela.
body.backTranslation: Check the rain of the place, frost, heat, soil and the availability of water before you choose plants.

body.text: Mango e ka senyehela ke serame. Quince e hloka winter chilling e loketseng bakeng sa kotulo e tshepehang.
body.backTranslation: Mango can be damaged by frost. Quince needs suitable winter chilling for a reliable harvest.

body.text: Lebitso la sebaka kapa sekgutlo se sirelelitsweng ha di lekane. Netefatsa semela se seng le se seng le mofuta ka tataiso e tshepehang ya sebaka.
body.backTranslation: The name of the place or a sheltered corner are not enough. Confirm each plant and species with reliable guidance for the place.

english.heading: Watch: Match the Species to the Climate
body: Climate decides which species belong.
On the Highveld, choose cold-tolerant trees and shrubs; on the KZN coast and Lowveld, choose warm-climate species.
Match every plant to your site.

heading.text: Sheba: Lekanya Mefuta le Boemo ba Leholimo

body.text: Boemo ba leholimo bo etsa qeto ya hore ke mefuta efe e loketseng.
body.backTranslation: Climate decides which species are suitable.

body.text: Highveld, kgetha difate le dihlahla tse mamellang bophodisa; KZN coast le Lowveld, kgetha mefuta ya dibaka tse mofuthu.
body.backTranslation: Highveld, choose trees and shrubs that tolerate cold; KZN coast and Lowveld, choose species of warm places.

body.text: Lekanya semela se seng le se seng le sebaka sa hao.
body.backTranslation: Match each plant with your place.

english.heading: Check the Highveld Examples
body: The original list includes pecan, walnut and indigenous fig; apple, pear, plum, black mulberry and loquat; rosemary, Wild Medlar, Cape gooseberry and Barbados cherry.
This list is not a blanket recommendation. Check each plant against frost, soil, mature size and the approved local species list.
Keep existing legal and project restrictions in force. Do not plant from a picture alone.

heading.text: Hlahloba Mehlala ya Highveld

body.text: Lenane la pele le kenyeletsa pecan, walnut le indigenous fig; apple, pear, plum, black mulberry le loquat; rosemary, Wild Medlar, Cape gooseberry le Barbados cherry.
body.backTranslation: The first list includes pecan, walnut and indigenous fig; apple, pear, plum, black mulberry and loquat; rosemary, Wild Medlar, Cape gooseberry and Barbados cherry.

body.text: Lenane lena ha se tlhahiso e sebetsang dibakeng tsohle. Hlahloba semela se seng le se seng ho latela serame, mobu, boholo ba ho hola ka botlalo le approved local species list.
body.backTranslation: This list is not a recommendation that works in all places. Check each plant according to frost, soil, size of growing fully and the approved local species list.

body.text: Boloka dithibelo tse teng tsa molao le tsa projeke di sebetsa. O se ke wa jala ka ho sheba setshwantsho feela.
body.backTranslation: Keep the existing restrictions of law and of the project in force. Do not plant by looking at a picture only.

english.heading: Check the Warm-Region Examples
body: The original warm-region examples include mango, avocado, Natal Mahogany, banana, pawpaw, litchi, Wild Fig, Barbados cherry and Wild Dagga.
Marula, Mopane and baobab also appear in the Limpopo examples. Local suitability still needs checking.
Useful trees are not automatically edible. Confirm identity and safe use; a landscape photograph is not a food-identification guide.

heading.text: Hlahloba Mehlala ya Dibaka tse Mofuthu

body.text: Mehlala ya pele ya dibaka tse mofuthu e kenyeletsa mango, avocado, Natal Mahogany, banana, pawpaw, litchi, Wild Fig, Barbados cherry le Wild Dagga.
body.backTranslation: First examples of warm places include mango, avocado, Natal Mahogany, banana, pawpaw, litchi, Wild Fig, Barbados cherry and Wild Dagga.

body.text: Marula, Mopane le baobab le tsona di hlaha mehlaleng ya Limpopo. Hore na di loketse sebaka ho sa hloka ho hlahlojwa.
body.backTranslation: Marula, Mopane and baobab also appear in the examples of Limpopo. Whether they are suitable for the place still needs to be checked.

body.text: Hore difate di na le molemo ha ho bolele hore di ka jewa. Netefatsa hore ke sefe le tshebediso e bolokehileng; setshwantsho sa naha ha se tataiso ya ho tseba hore ke dijo dife.
body.backTranslation: Even though trees have benefit, it does not mean that they can be eaten. Confirm which one it is and its safe use; a picture of the land is not a guide to knowing which are foods.

english.heading: Include Locally Appropriate Indigenous Plants
body: Locally appropriate indigenous plants can support habitat as part of the design.
Choose for your ecosystem and the useful role of each plant. There is no sourced percentage target in this lesson.
Protect existing natural vegetation. Do not turn healthy grassland into a food forest simply because trees are useful elsewhere.

heading.text: Kenya Dimela tsa Indigenous tse Loketseng Sebaka
heading.backTranslation: Bring in Indigenous Plants Suitable for the Place

body.text: Dimela tsa indigenous tse loketseng sebaka sa heno di ka tshehetsa habitat e le karolo ya moralo.
body.backTranslation: Indigenous plants suitable for your place can support habitat as a part of the design.

body.text: Kgetha ho latela ecosystem ya hao le tshebetso e molemo ya semela se seng le se seng. Thutong ena ha ho na nepo ya diperesente e nang le mohlodi.
body.backTranslation: Choose according to your ecosystem and the good function of each plant. In this course there is no percentage target that has a source.

body.text: Sireletsa dimela tsa tlhaho tse teng. O se ke wa fetola naha ya joang e phetseng hantle hore e be food forest feela ka lebaka la hore difate di na le molemo dibakeng tse ding.
body.backTranslation: Protect the natural plants that are already there. Do not change grassland that is living/growing well [?healthy] so that it becomes a food forest only because trees have benefit in other places.

english.heading: Plan the Sequence for the Site
body: Start by checking the site, water supply and care available. Protect exposed soil early.
Temporary support plants may provide shelter and useful cut material where appropriate.
Main trees and lower layers can be introduced as conditions allow. Ground cover need not wait until the end; avoid plants competing with young trees.

heading.text: Rala Tatellano bakeng sa Sebaka
heading.backTranslation: Design a Sequence for the Place

body.text: Qala ka ho hlahloba sebaka, tlhahiso ya metsi le tlhokomelo e teng. Sireletsa mobu o pepeneneng kapele.
body.backTranslation: Start by checking the place, the supply of water and the care that is there. Protect bare soil quickly.

body.text: Support plants tsa nakwana di ka fana ka tshireletso le thepa e sehilweng e sebetsang moo ho loketseng.
body.backTranslation: Temporary support plants can give protection and cut material that works where suitable.

body.text: Difate tse ka sehlooho le mekgahlelo e ka tlase di ka kenngwa ha maemo a dumella. Dimela tse kwahelang mobu ha di hloke ho emela ho fihlela qetellong; qoba hore dimela di phehisane le difate tse nyane.
body.backTranslation: Main trees and the lower layers can be put in when conditions allow. Plants that cover the soil do not need to wait until the end; avoid having plants compete with small trees.

english.heading: Watch: Care for a Young Food Forest
body: This picture shows a young food forest. Start with an area you can care for.
Protect exposed soil early. Here, loose mulch covers the soil.
Keep mulch away from the trunk. Notice the clear space at the tree's base.
Watch for competition. The farmer is removing grass near the young tree.
Before adding more plants, check moisture, shelter and the care you can provide. Let what you observe guide your next step.

heading.text: Sheba: Hlokomela Food Forest e Sa Tswa Jalwa
heading.backTranslation: Look: Care for a Newly Planted Food Forest

body.text: Setshwantsho sena se bontsha food forest e sa le nyane. Qala ka sebaka seo o ka se hlokomelang.
body.backTranslation: This picture shows a food forest that is still small. Start with a place that you can look after.

body.text: Sireletsa mobu o pepeneneng kapele. Mona, mulch e lokolohileng e kwahela mobu.
body.backTranslation: Protect bare soil quickly. Here, loose mulch covers the soil.

body.text: Boloka mulch kgole le kutu ya sefate. Sheba sebaka se hlakileng botlaseng ba sefate.
body.backTranslation: Keep mulch far from the trunk of the tree. Look at the clear space at the bottom of the tree.

body.text: Elellwa ho phehisana. Molemi o tlosa joang haufi le sefate se senyane.
body.backTranslation: Be aware of competition. The farmer removes grass near the small tree.

body.text: Pele o eketsa dimela tse ding, hlahloba mongobo, tshireletso le tlhokomelo eo o ka e fanang. Tlohela seo o se bonang se tataise mohato o latelang.
body.backTranslation: Before you add other plants, check moisture, protection and the care you can give. Let what you see guide the next step.

english.heading: Prepare a Manageable First Area
body: Begin with an area you can water and maintain. Check existing vegetation before clearing.
Where appropriate, plain cardboard under suitable mulch can suppress unwanted growth. Keep water able to enter the soil and leave trunks clear.
Plan spacing from mature plant size. Prepare nursery plants for the next suitable planting opportunity.

heading.text: Lokisa Sebaka sa Pele se Laolehang

body.text: Qala ka sebaka seo o ka se nosetsang le ho se hlokomela. Hlahloba dimela tse teng pele o di tlosa.
body.backTranslation: Start with an area that you can water and care for. Check the plants that are there before you remove them.

body.text: Moo ho loketseng, cardboard e se nang kgatiso ka tlasa mulch e loketseng e ka thiba kgolo e sa batleheng. Dumella metsi hore a kene mobung mme o tlohele dikutu di hlakile.
body.backTranslation: Where suitable, cardboard without printing below suitable mulch can block unwanted growth. Allow water to enter the soil and leave the stems clear.

body.text: Rala sebaka pakeng tsa dimela ho latela boholo ba tsona ha di hola ka botlalo. Lokisa nursery plants bakeng sa monyetla o latelang o loketseng wa ho jala.
body.backTranslation: Plan the space between plants according to their size when they have grown fully. Prepare nursery plants for the next suitable opportunity of planting.

english.heading: Adjust as the Trees Grow
body: Watch how shade, roots and available water affect neighbouring plants.
Comfrey and wild garlic appear in the original underplanting example; check their local suitability before use.
Prune or thin support plants when needed, using methods suited to each species. Suitable clean cuttings can return as mulch. Do not wait for a fixed year if competition is already harming plants.

heading.text: Fetola ha Difate di Ntse di Hola

body.text: Elellwa hore moriti, metso le metsi a teng di ama jwang dimela tse haufi.
body.backTranslation: Be aware of how shade, roots and the water that is there affect nearby plants.

body.text: Comfrey le wild garlic di hlaha mohlalong wa pele wa dimela tse jetsweng ka tlasa difate; hlahloba hore na di loketse sebaka pele o di sebedisa.
body.backTranslation: Comfrey and wild garlic appear in the first example of plants planted below trees; check whether they suit the place before you use them.

body.text: Seha makala kapa etsa thinning ya support plants ha ho hlokeha, o sebedisa mekgwa e loketseng mofuta o mong le o mong. Makala a sehilweng a hlwekileng a loketseng a ka kgutlela e le mulch. O se ke wa emela selemo se tsitsitseng haeba ho phehisana ho se ho senya dimela.
body.backTranslation: Cut branches or do thinning of support plants when needed, using methods suitable to each species. Clean cut branches that are suitable can return as mulch. Do not wait for a fixed year if competition is already damaging plants.

english.heading: Plant with Reliable Moisture
body: Choose a planting opportunity when soil moisture and expected weather support establishment.
Rain can help, but check the root zone and keep a backup watering plan. Avoid planting into waterlogged ground.
Check young plants after planting. Harvest timing and outside inputs depend on the species, site and care; there is no guaranteed fifth-year result.

heading.text: Jala ha Mongobo o Tshepehile

body.text: Kgetha monyetla wa ho jala ha mongobo wa mobu le maemo a leholimo a lebelletsweng a thusa nako ya pele kamora ho jala (establishment).
body.backTranslation: Choose an opportunity of planting where the moisture of the soil and the expected conditions of the weather help the early period after planting.

body.text: Pula e ka thusa, empa hlahloba root zone mme o boloke leano la bobedi la ho nosetsa. Qoba ho jala mobung o tletseng metsi.
body.backTranslation: Rain can help, but check the root zone and keep a second plan of watering. Avoid planting in soil that is full of water.

body.text: Hlahloba dimela tse nyane kamora ho jala. Nako ya kotulo le dintho tse tswang kantle di ipapisitse le mofuta, sebaka le tlhokomelo; ha ho na tiisetso ya sephetho selemong sa bohlano.
body.backTranslation: Check the small plants after planting. Harvest time and things that come from outside depend on the kind, the place and the care; there is no guarantee of a result in the fifth year.

english.heading: Field Assignment
body: Draw the layers for your own proposed planting. Mark access, water and existing natural vegetation.
Record local frost, rain, soil and available care.
For each plant from the approved list, record its intended role and the local advice still needed before planting.

heading.text: Mosebetsi wa Tshimong

body.text: Taka mekgahlelo bakeng sa ho jala hoo o ho rerileng. Tshwaya phihlello, metsi le dimela tsa tlhaho tse teng.
body.backTranslation: Draw layers for the planting that you have planned. Mark access, water and the natural plants that are there.

body.text: Ngola serame, pula, mobu le tlhokomelo e fumanehang sebakeng sa heno.
body.backTranslation: Write down frost, rain, soil and care that are available in your place.

body.text: Bakeng sa semela se seng le se seng lenaneng le dumeletsweng, ngola tshebetso eo se e reretsweng le keletso e amanang le sebaka sa heno e ntseng e hlokeha pele o jala.
body.backTranslation: For each plant in the permitted list, write the function it is intended for and the advice related to your place/area that is still needed before you plant.

english.heading: Field Action
body: Inspect a manageable area and choose one next step.
Protect exposed soil, check plant suitability, or prepare nursery plants.
Plant only when conditions and follow-up care are suitable. Return to the same spot to check survival, soil moisture and competition.

heading.text: Ketso ya Tshimong

body.text: Hlahloba karolo ya sebaka seo o ka se hlokomelang, ebe o kgetha mohato o le mong o latelang.
body.backTranslation: Check the part of the place that you can care for, then choose one next step.

body.text: Sireletsa mobu o pepeneneng, hlahloba hore dimela di loketse sebaka, kapa lokisa dimela tsa nursery.
body.backTranslation: Protect bare soil, check that plants suit the place, or prepare nursery plants.

body.text: Jala feela ha maemo le tlhokomelo e latelang di loketse. Kgutlela sebakeng se le seng ho hlahloba hore na dimela di phetse, mongobo wa mobu le ho phehisana.
body.backTranslation: Plant only when conditions and the care that follows are suitable. Return to the same place to check whether the plants are alive, the moisture of the soil and competition.
